newsitem.title: USA: Doctors can get rid of four tropical diseases.
newsitem.headline: Doctors can get rid of four tropical diseases.

text.p: Developing countries should be able to get rid of four major tropical diseases within 10 years with investments in cheap drugs and new insecticides, medical researchers said on Saturday.

Millions of people are at risk from the four diseases, leprosy, river blindness, Chagas disease and lymphatic filariasis, according to the Special Program for Research and Training in Tropical Diseases (TDR).
The public health scourges can be controlled thanks to treatments developed over the last 20 years, insect-killing bacteria, simple insecticides, and new mapping programs to track diseases.

"We now have an historic opportunity ... to eliminate these diseases," said Tore Godal, director of TDR, which is funded by the World Health Organization, the United Nations Development Program, and World Bank.
The TDR report estimated it would cost $370 million over the next four years to help eliminate leprosy, a severely deforming disease caused by bacteria.

More than half a million new leprosy cases are reported annually in 60 countries in Southeast Asia, Africa and Latin America, according to WHO. The TDR report said a treatment involving three drugs "is able to cure all patients."

"The greatest challenges for eliminating leprosy will come in India and Brazil and in countries where civil strife and wars prevent us from reaching the affected populations," said Shaik Noordeen, director of the leprosy program.
River blindness, caused by a parasite transmitted to humans through blackflies, has afflicted about 18 million people mainly in Africa.

The drug ivermectin has been used to kill the larvae released by adult worms in tissue under the skin, helping to prevent blindness and skin lesions. But scientists are still looking for a way to kill the adult worms.
Ivermectin combined with another drug has also been used successfully to treat lymphatic filariasis.

The disease, which affects 120 million people in 73 tropical and subtropical countries, is passed on by mosquitoes infected with worm larvae that block the lymphatic system, grossly enlarging legs and genitals, and damaging lungs.

Chagas disease, which kills about 45,000 people a year in Latin America, is transmitted to humans by a bloodsucking insect that lives in cracks in the walls of low-quality homes. The disease can now be treated for just 5 cents per person.

Instead of spraying insecticides to get rid of the carrier bugs, scientists have developed a latex-based paint with insecticides that is effective for two years. A new fumigant is also being tested in Argentina.
